videos.summary:

I'm chasing a cheat curl record, so I take you through my warm-up, my heavy attempts, and how I deal with the doubt that creeps in before a big lift. A short prayer before each attempt keeps me calm, and calm is where my best strength comes out. Not every rep went my way, but I left happy with the numbers two nights in a row.

What's in this one:
- Training biceps for armwrestling with heavy cheat curls
- Warming up and working up to big attempts
- Handling self-doubt and anxiety before a heavy lift
- Why staying calm matters more than forcing it

videos.title: Overpronating in Armwrestling: Why Taking the Wrist Isn't Enough
videos.summary:
Overpronating in armwrestling: winning your opponent's wrist is not the same as winning the match, and running your top roll too far can leave you with almost nothing.

In this one I put myself against myself on a crane scale to show the difference between an over-pronated, over-top-rolled position and the position of a puller who has lost his wrist. The gap in side pressure surprised even me. Then I walk through how to fix your top roll so you stay close to the fight and can actually finish.

What I cover:
- What overpronating and over top rolling really are, and why I still see it at the pro level
- The crane scale test: side pressure when over-pronated and outside the shoulder versus palm-up with the wrist lost
- Why beginners may give up once their wrist folds, but developed pullers will out-press you from there
- Keeping your fingers in contact with strong, hooked deadlifting fingers instead of aggressive curling
- Finishing your top roll in front of your shoulder rather than drifting outside it
- How to absorb their side pressure, rise, cup deep and derail before you finish with a top roll or press

Have you ever won someone's wrist and still lost the match? Tell me in the comments.

videos.title: What happened against Cvetan Gashevski
videos.summary:
What happens when you try to beat one of the best King's movers in armwrestling with an untested theory? My match against Cvetan Gashevski became the most exhausting, and most fascinating, of my career.

Many of you asked what happened, so here is my breakdown. Instead of the usual approach of out-rising Cvetan and breaking his wrist, I wanted to test my black hole idea against his constant back pressure. It didn't go to plan, and I explain why and what I'd do differently next time.

What I cover:
- Why Cvetan's back pressure is so hard to deal with compared to most pullers
- The normal way people try to beat a King's mover, and why I chose not to
- What the black hole is: pressing toward him and lowering my arm to drag him into his own cup
- Getting partway there before my hand pumped out
- How rounds two and three played out, including my own King's move attempt
- My plan for a rematch: an aggressive back pressure top roll, or refining the black hole

How would you have pulled against Cvetan? Tell me in the comments.
